answerBody:
The final rule should preserve local control as the governing default, with federal preemption available only after a concrete showing that a particular deadline failure, fee, moratorium, or condition materially inhibits service. The FCC can and should create rebuttable presumptions to make that showing practical, but it should not make displacement of local rights-of-way authority the ordinary consequence of delay or disputed cost.

That default best fits the statute. Section 253(a) of the Communications Act bars state or local requirements that prohibit, or have the effect of prohibiting, telecommunications service. But Section 253(c) expressly protects local authority to manage public rights-of-way and to require fair, reasonable, publicly disclosed, competitively neutral, and nondiscriminatory compensation. The FCC’s August 7, 2026 Federal Register notice, “Build America: Eliminating Barriers to Wireline Deployments,” proposes a 120-day presumption and cost-based fee limits because some approvals reportedly take months or years and can cancel or shrink projects. Those facts justify a faster evidentiary path; they do not erase Congress’s preserved local role.

A preemption-by-default rule would also be legally and operationally fragile. Rights-of-way are not empty corridors. They contain water, gas, electric, drainage, traffic-control, and public-safety systems; the same trench that is routine in one town may be dangerous or expensive in another. Local governments are normally best positioned to sequence street cuts, protect recently paved roads, coordinate emergency access, and require restoration. The National Association of Counties’ 2026 opposition statement overstates the case if it treats every federal shot clock as unsafe, but it correctly identifies the public-safety and asset-management functions that Section 253(c) preserves.

The strongest argument for a preemption default is serious: broadband networks are interstate infrastructure, federal BEAD subsidies are now moving into construction, and a locality can extract monopoly rents simply by controlling the last mile of permission. The FCC’s record, as summarized in its June 2026 release, says some governments act promptly while others delay, demand in-kind concessions, or layer approvals until builds become uneconomic. The Ninth Circuit’s 2020 City of Portland decision also upheld the FCC’s use of actual, direct costs as a reasonable anchor for wireless small-cell fees, rejecting the idea that localities must be allowed profit-like rents from rights-of-way.

But that supports a burden-shifting rule, not automatic preemption. Missing 120 days should create a prima facie Section 253 problem; fees above safe harbors should require documented actual and direct costs; in-kind demands should count against fee limits; and repeated unexplained delay should support targeted preemption or expedited court/FCC relief. Localities should be able to rebut with project-specific facts: incomplete applications, provider-caused sequencing delays, winter construction bans, railroad or environmental dependencies, emergency work, unusual traffic impacts, or documented restoration costs.

The conclusion-changing evidence would be a record showing that case-specific review routinely fails because litigation costs or timing make relief worthless. On the present record, the better default is disciplined local control: federal standards, presumptions, transparency, and targeted preemption when a specific local act blocks service.
rationale: The answer is based on independent review of the FCC’s 2026 wireline rights-of-way proposal, Section 253, relevant appellate treatment of cost-based fee limits, BEAD deployment context, and local-government objections. It chooses and defends a governing default while addressing the strongest counterargument and uncertainty.
